extracted.intended_audience: USPTO patent examiners (and patent practitioners reviewing SME practice)
extracted.subtask_description: A step‑by‑step worksheet for analyzing claim subject‑matter eligibility under 35 U.S.C. 101 (judicial exceptions: law of nature, natural phenomenon, abstract idea) following the 2014 Interim Eligibility Guidance and related updates. It guides examiners through claim construction, Step 1 (statutory category), Step 2A (directed to abstract idea), and Step 2B (significantly more/inventive concept).

rubrics_metrics.name: Identify what applicant invented and review the disclosure (Section I)
rubrics_metrics.description: Review the disclosure to identify what applicant considers as the invention. (MPEP 2103(I))
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use the disclosure to state what applicant invented (example language: 'a graphical user interface for dynamically relocating/rescaling obscured textual information ...'). This informs the analysis of additional elements and inventive concept in later steps. As every claim must be examined individually, use a separate worksheet for each claim. The worksheet use is optional.

rubrics_metrics.name: Establish the broadest reasonable interpretation (BRI) of the claim
rubrics_metrics.description: Establish the broadest reasonable interpretation (BRI) of the claim before conducting SME analysis.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Conceive the claim under BRI in view of the background; determine what claim limitations would require (e.g., 'generating' steps may require calculating areas). Clarify the record in the Office action if necessary (e.g., state that the BRI is not directed to an abstract idea). See MPEP references.

rubrics_metrics.name: Step 1 — Statutory category check (process, machine, manufacture, composition)
rubrics_metrics.description: Does the claimed invention fall within one of the four statutory categories of invention (process, machine, manufacture or composition of matter)?
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Choose A or B: A. Yes — continue SME analysis. B. No — make a rejection of the claim as being drawn to non‑statutory subject matter (use Form Paragraphs 7.05 and 7.05.01). If an amendment could render the claim statutory, consider proceeding with the analysis under that assumption and make the assumption clear in the record; suggest potential amendments.

rubrics_metrics.name: Step 2A — Determine whether the claim is directed to an abstract idea
rubrics_metrics.description: Identify whether the claim recites a concept similar to judicially identified abstract ideas (e.g., fundamental economic practices, methods of organizing human activity, ideas themselves, mathematical relationships/formulae). 'A claim is “directed” to an abstract idea when the abstract idea is recited ... in the claim.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Choose A, B, or C: A. No — conclude SME analysis. B. Yes, but streamlined analysis appropriate — eligibility is self‑evident; no full analysis needed (refer to February 2015 Training Slides). C. Yes — identify limitation(s) that recite the abstract idea and explain the similarity to court examples (refer to July 2015 Update Quick Reference Sheet). Provide explanation linking claim limitations to judicial exceptions (e.g., steps that calculate areas and a scaling factor are mathematical relationships/algorithms).

rubrics_metrics.name: Identify claim limitations that correspond to the abstract idea
rubrics_metrics.description: Point to the specific limitation(s) in the claim that set forth or describe the abstract idea and explain why they are abstract.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Explicitly identify the limitation text (for example: 'generating first and second data ... calculating a scaling factor proportional to the difference between the first data and the second data'). Explain how these recite mathematical relationships/algorithms or other judicial exceptions, and cite controlling cases (e.g., Benson, Flook, Diehr, Grams) as appropriate.

rubrics_metrics.name: Streamlined analysis option when eligibility is self‑evident
rubrics_metrics.description: Where the eligibility determination is self‑evident and the claim does not attempt to tie up an abstract idea, a full eligibility analysis may not be needed.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If using streamlined analysis (Step 2A choice B), state why the claim is not focused on the abstract idea and why it does not prevent others from practicing the abstract idea. Refer to February 2015 Training Slides for examples.

rubrics_metrics.name: Step 2B — Identify additional elements beyond the abstract idea
rubrics_metrics.description: Are there any additional elements (features/limitations/steps) recited in the claim beyond the abstract idea identified in Step 2A?
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Choose 1 or 2: 1. No — conclude SME analysis by making a § 101 rejection and use Form Paragraphs 7.05 and 7.05.015. Identify any elements in the disclosure that could be added to make it eligible and consider suggesting them. 2. Yes — list the additional claim elements (e.g., 'computer with a screen and a processor', 'displaying first and second windows', 'constantly monitoring boundaries', 'scaling and relocating textual information', 'automatically returning textual information'). Continue to evaluate their significance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Evaluate significance of additional elements (search for inventive concept)
rubrics_metrics.description: Consider whether the additional elements, individually or in combination, result in the claim amounting to significantly more than the abstract idea (i.e., whether there is an 'inventive concept').
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Reasons that can support significance include one or more of the following: improves another technology/technical field; improves the functioning of a computer itself; applies the abstract idea with, or by use of, a particular machine (not a generic computer performing generic functions); effects a transformation or reduction of a particular article to a different state; adds a specific limitation other than what is well‑understood, routine and conventional; adds unconventional steps that confine the claim to a particular useful application; adds meaningful limitations beyond merely linking to a technological environment. Anti‑patterns: generic computer performing generic functions, merely adding the words 'apply it', appending well‑understood/routine/conventional activities at a high level, adding insignificant extrasolution activity (mere data gathering).

rubrics_metrics.name: Consider claim preamble and 'computer‑implemented' limitations when construing scope
rubrics_metrics.description: Treat computer‑implemented limitations (e.g., 'the computer', references in preamble) as giving 'life, meaning and vitality' to the preamble when appropriate (see MPEP 2111.02).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A preamble that is given weight can further limit the claim and may be relevant to whether additional elements amount to significantly more. However, simply stating 'computer‑implemented' or 'by the computer' is often akin to adding the words 'apply it' to a claim and may not be sufficient.

rubrics_metrics.name: Conclude eligibility or issue § 101 rejection with articulated reasoning
rubrics_metrics.description: If additional elements amount to significantly more, conclude SME analysis and continue with examination. If not, make a § 101 rejection.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If concluding ineligibility, use sample rejection language (examples provided), use Form Paragraphs 7.05 and 7.05.015, and clearly articulate why the claimed invention is directed to a judicial exception without significantly more. The examiner's burden is met by clearly articulating the reasons why the claimed invention is not eligible. Although factual evidence is not required for a prima facie rejection, examiners are encouraged to cite any additional resources that support their rejections.

rubrics_metrics.name: Suggest possible claim amendments to confer eligibility
rubrics_metrics.description: Identify elements in the disclosure that could be added to the claim that may make it eligible and consider suggesting them to applicant.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Provide concrete suggested claim elements or point to example claims in the application that demonstrate how added limitations produced eligibility (e.g., see Example 23 claim 4). Document such suggestions in the Office action record when appropriate.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of form paragraphs and recordkeeping guidance
rubrics_metrics.description: When issuing rejections or following assumptions (e.g., assuming claim amended to fall within statutory category), use the specified form paragraphs and make the assumptions clear in the record.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: References in the worksheet: use Form Paragraphs 7.05, 7.05.01, 7.05.015 available in Custom OACs for § 101 rejections or notices. If proceeding under an assumption that an amendment makes the claim statutory, state the assumption in the record and consider suggesting potential amendments to applicant.

rubrics_metrics.name: Illustrative examples and precedent citation
rubrics_metrics.description: When explaining why limitations are abstract or why additional elements are/are not significant, rely on judicial precedent and illustrative examples.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Cite cases such as Benson, Flook, Diehr, Grams where mathematical procedures/algorithms were treated as abstract ideas. Use the Quick Reference Sheet (July 2015 Update) and Training Slides (February 2015) for examples and to support whether a concept is an abstract idea or whether additional elements provide significantly more.
